plain_english: I believe — though my Stoic friends wouldn't like hearing this — that Epicurus taught something upright and holy. If you look closely, his teaching was actually quite strict. The pleasure he talks about gets squeezed down to very little. He tells pleasure to follow the same rule we tell virtue to follow: obey nature. But luxury won't settle for what nature needs. What happens then? Anyone who thinks happiness means lazy lounging around, stuffing themselves, then indulging in vice — well, they need a good excuse for bad behavior. When they become "Epicureans" (drawn by the appealing name), they don't follow the pleasure Epicurus actually taught. They follow the pleasure they brought with them. Once they convince themselves their vices match this philosophy, they stop hiding their bad behavior in dark corners. Now they do it boldly, right out in the open.
original_excerpt: I myself believe, though my Stoic comrades would be unwilling to hear me say so, that the teaching of Epicurus was upright and holy, and even, if you examine it narrowly, stern: for this much talked of pleasure is reduced to a very narrow compass, and he bids pleasure submit to the same law which we bid virtue do—I mean, to obey nature. Luxury, however, is not satisfied with what is enough for nature. What is the consequence? Whoever thinks that happiness consists in lazy sloth, and alternations of gluttony and profligacy, requires a good patron for a bad action, and when he has become an Epicurean, having been led to do so by the attractive name of that school, he follows, not the pleasure which he there hears spoken of, but that which he brought thither with him, and, haying learned to think that his vices coincide with the maxims of that philosophy, he indulges in them no longer timidly and in dark corners, but boldly in the face of day.

plain_english: I won't say what most of my fellow Stoics say — that Epicurus teaches people to be criminals. What I will say is this: his philosophy gets a bad reputation, even though it doesn't deserve one. "But how can anyone judge it without studying it deeply?" The problem is how it looks from the outside. It gives people an excuse to be scandalous and feeds their worst desires. It's like a brave warrior dressed in women's clothes. Your honor might be intact, your courage might be real, you might do nothing shameful — but you're still holding a tambourine like some religious dancer. So choose a better motto for your school. Pick something that lifts people up on its own. The sign hanging over your door right now was written by vice itself.
original_excerpt: I will not, therefore, like most of our school, say that the sect of Epicurus is the teacher of crime, but what I say is: it is ill spoken of, it has a bad reputation, and yet it does not deserve it. "Who can know this without having been admitted to its inner mysteries?" Its very outside gives opportunity for scandal, and encourages men's baser desires: it is like a brave man dressed in a woman's gown: your chastity is assured, your manhood is safe, your body is submitted to nothing disgraceful, but your hand holds a drum (like a priest of Cybele). Choose, then, some honourable superscription for your school, some writing which shall in itself arouse the mind: that which at present stands over your door has been invented by the vices.

plain_english: When you choose virtue, you show that you have a noble character. When you chase pleasure, you look weak, worn out, and degraded. You're likely to fall into shameful vices unless someone helps you sort out which pleasures are okay and which aren't. Some pleasures stay within natural limits. Others are wild and endless — the more you feed them, the hungrier they get. But listen! Let virtue lead the way. Then every step you take will be safe. Too much pleasure hurts you. But with virtue, you never need to worry about having too much. Virtue already contains moderation within itself. Anything that gets damaged by its own excess can't be truly good. Besides, what better guide could there be for reasoning creatures like us than reason itself? So if this appeals to you — if you want to move toward happiness this way — let virtue lead and let pleasure follow behind like a shadow hanging around your body. Only a mind that can't handle great things would make virtue into pleasure's servant.
original_excerpt: He who ranges himself on the side of virtue gives thereby a proof of a noble disposition: he who follows pleasure appears to be weakly, worn out, degrading his manhood, likely to fall into infamous vices unless someone discriminates his pleasures for him, so that he may know which remain within the bounds of natural desire, which are frantic and boundless, and become all the more insatiable the more they are satisfied. But come! let virtue lead the way: then every step will be safe. Too much pleasure is hurtful: but with virtue we need fear no excess of any kind, because moderation is contained in virtue herself. That which is injured by its own extent cannot be a good thing: besides, what better guide can there be than reason for beings endowed with a reasoning nature? so if this combination pleases you, if you are willing to proceed to a happy life thus accompanied, let virtue lead the way, let pleasure follow and hang about the body like a shadow: it is the part of a mind incapable of great things to hand over virtue, the highest of all qualities, as a handmaid to pleasure.
